query: Earlier studies on stainless, alloy, and boiler steels reported improved hardness, wear resistance, thermal stability, or reduced mass change during aggressive salt exposure at 700–900 °C. However, these findings were specific to individual material systems and emphasized characterization or performance rather than establishing why corrosion protection persists or fails across room- and high-temperature regimes; studies combining HEAs, subsequent annealing, and hot-corrosion assessment were also reported to be minimal. For Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain its corrosion-related degradation or retention of protection under these regimes? Specify a controlled study that would isolate the governing cause, predicted observations relative to an appropriate reference, the conditions under which the hypothesis should and should not apply, supporting evidence from the earlier studies, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The integrity of an in situ formed iron oxide passivating film on pre-exposure Q235 steel governs its corrosion protection; while a thin, adherent Fe2O3/Fe3O4 layer is effective at room temperature, high-temperature exposure induces increased oxidation kinetics and thermal stress that cause the film to thicken and ultimately spall, thereby compromising protection.
generation.material_initial_state: Q235 carbon steel in its as-received condition, featuring a native, thin iron oxide layer formed during storage and handling.
generation.intervention: Expose Q235 samples to aggressive salt environments at room temperature and at high temperatures (700–900 °C), monitoring the evolution of the oxide film over time.
generation.conditions: Testing in controlled atmospheres containing aggressive halide or sulfate salts; experiments conducted both at ambient temperatures and under high-temperature conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation, growth, and adhesion of the surface iron oxide scale, primarily composed of Fe2O3/Fe3O4.
generation.mechanism: At room temperature, a thin, adherent iron oxide film forms that passivates the surface and inhibits further corrosion; at high temperatures, faster oxidation kinetics, coupled with thermal expansion mismatches and stresses, lead to a thickening and eventual spallation of the oxide scale, thereby exposing fresh metal and accelerating corrosion.
generation.predicted_outcome: Room-temperature samples maintain low corrosion rates with an intact passivating oxide film, whereas high-temperature samples exhibit non-uniform, spalled oxide scales accompanied by marked increases in mass change and surface degradation.
generation.baseline: Unmodified Q235 steel with its native oxide characteristics established via baseline XRD/EDS and microscopy prior to high-temperature exposure.
generation.boundary: This mechanism pertains primarily to low-alloy carbon steels lacking additional elements that stabilize the oxide film; it is less applicable to advanced alloys with superior high-temperature oxidation resistance.
generation.uncertainty: The exact kinetics of oxide scale thickening and spallation under molten salt conditions in Q235 steel are not fully established, leaving uncertainty in the precise temperature thresholds involved.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform comparative salt immersion tests on Q235 steel at room temperature and at high temperatures; characterize the oxide film using XRD, EDS, and electron microscopy at various time points, and measure overall mass change.
measurements: Phase composition and thickness of the oxide film (XRD, EDS)
Scale adhesion and morphology (optical and electron microscopy)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If high-temperature samples display a continuous, well-adherent oxide film with corrosion rates comparable to room-temperature samples, then the proposed mechanism of oxide film breakdown due to thermal stresses is disproven.

cited_evidence.text: The trace elemental analysis (Table 1) showed that, although both HEA and 316 H stainless steel alloys have almost the same Cr concentration (~18 wt.%), the HEA alloy lost significantly lower amount of Cr to the salt compared to the 316 H stainless steel. This is due to the presence of Mn in the HEA that hinders the dissolution of Cr in the salt. Even for the 316 H stainless steel which contains an appreciably lower Mn concentration (maximum 2 wt.%), Mn dissolution was observed raising its concentration in the salt from 4 to 40 ppm after the corrosion test. These results may be explained by the lower standard Gibbs free energy of formation of MnF2 compared to CrF2, as shown in Fig. 8, which suggests that Mn would tend to dissolve in molten fluoride salt rather than Cr. In addition, the mass change measurements (Fig. 4) showed that the HEA has a higher mass loss compared to the 316 H stainless steel alloy, which indicates a higher dissolution rate of Mn compared to Cr, likely due to the higher diffusion coefficient of Mn in these systems,. The combination of lower standard Gibbs free energy and high diffusion coefficient of Mn relative to Cr, led to the higher dissolution rate of Mn

Following the significant Mn dissolution from the alloy into the salt to form MnF2, the Mn/MnF2 redox couple could become a salt redox buffer, and thus the immersed sample, would then be fixed at this buffer level. At this potential, the Cr becomes a noble element with respect to the salt, and Cr dissolution would not be thermodynamically favorable. It is not known how much Mn in the salt is required to reach a satisfactory buffer level, but that would be an interesting point to study in the future. These observations point to the possibility of using Mn/MnF2 couple as a redox buffer to reduce the overall corrosion potential and to slow or stop the dissolution of Cr. Such technique, in principle, was employed in the MSR experiment in ORNL during the 1960s by adding metallic elements such as Mg, Zr, and Be to the salt,. However, in our case, the structural materials would provide a constant source of buffer to the salt. Another possible mechanism is that adding Mn to the alloy in molten salt environment could act as a sacrificial mechanism to protect the Cr content. This is relatively different from aqueous sacrificial protection mechanism, where Mn would be added as a pure Mn bar i

candidates.hypothesis: At high temperatures (700–900 °C), enhanced grain-boundary diffusion in Q235 steel accelerates the selective dissolution of alloying elements (notably Fe and minor Mn), leading to localized dealloying that disrupts the protective oxide film and accelerates corrosion, whereas at room temperature, limited diffusion preserves the passivating layer.
candidates.intervention: Expose Q235 samples to identical aggressive salt environments at room temperature and at 700–900 °C, and perform high-resolution elemental mapping along grain boundaries to assess diffusion and depletion rates.
candidates.changes: Replaced the original grain-boundary precipitate mechanism—deemed poorly supported for Q235—with a diffusion-controlled dealloying mechanism that attributes high-temperature corrosion to accelerated grain-boundary diffusion leading to selective elemental depletion and oxide breakdown.

candidates.hypothesis: Residual stresses imparted during manufacturing enhance the adhesion and integrity of the native oxide scale on Q235 steel at room temperature, but upon exposure to 700–900 °C, stress relaxation reduces the mechanical support for the oxide film, resulting in spallation and accelerated corrosion.
candidates.intervention: Compare the corrosion performance of as-received Q235 steel with samples that have undergone full stress-relief annealing before salt exposure at both room temperature and 700–900 °C.
candidates.changes: Expanded the discussion on residual stress effects by detailing measurement techniques and linking stress relaxation to reduced oxide film adhesion. This addresses reviewer concerns regarding quantification and specificity.
